correctness.rationale: Equation \(3\sigma(m)=4m+d\) is exact for \(n=2m\) with odd \(m\). The parity characterization of \(\sigma(m)\), the divisor constraint \(d\mid2m\), and the lifting identity for \(v_2(\sigma(p^a))\) together prove every quantified branch. The bundled checker independently enumerates all integers through \(2{,}000{,}000\) and finds no counterexample; this finite check is explicitly non-probative for the infinite statement.

evidence: Pollack--Shevelev conjectures restrictions when an even near-perfect number has an odd redundant divisor; it does not prove that, inside \(v_2(n)=1\), odd redundant divisor is equivalent to square odd part.
Ren--Chen's theorem implies the \(\omega(n)=2\) instances only after using their full classification; it does not cover 234 or 650 structurally, much less arbitrary support.
The current proof uses only the defining divisor-sum equation, parity, multiplicativity, and the exact 2-adic valuation of a geometric sum.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: No checked prior theorem implies the full arbitrary-support dichotomy. Known special-support classifications intersect it but do not dominate it, while the odd-redundant-divisor conjecture is weaker and unproved in general.

evidence: Pollack--Shevelev, arXiv:1011.6160, studies near-perfect constructions and odd redundant divisors but does not state this valuation-one shape theorem.

It concerns even numbers with exactly one factor of two and derives a dichotomy for all odd-prime exponents plus the parity of the redundant divisor. No equivalent formulation was found in the inspected sources or exact-phrase searches.

value.rationale: The theorem gives a uniform structural restriction for the natural, previously unclassified slice \(v_2(n)=1\) at arbitrary odd-prime support. It converts near-perfectness into a one-odd-exponent rule with exact mod-4 constraints and simultaneously identifies when the redundant divisor can be odd. This supplies a reusable filter for classification and explains multiple early three-prime examples, rather than merely checking finitely many terms.
